{{smaller block|<poem>He did not pause to parley nor protest,
But hastened to obey the Lord’s ''behest.''</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Torquemada.}}}}

'''behest†''' (bē-hest′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''behesten'', promise, < ''beheste'', a promise: see ''behest'', ''n.''] To promise; vow.

'''behete†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''behight.''

'''behew†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''behewen'', hew about, carve, < AS. ''beheáwan'', hew off, < ''be-'' (in AS. priv.) + ''heáwan'', cut, hew.] To carve; adorn; embellish.
{{smaller block|Al with gold ''behewe.'' ''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1306.}}

'''behight†''' (bē-hīt′), ''v.'' [The common spelling in Spenser and his contemporaries of both present and preterit of ME. pres. inf. ''beheten'', regularly ''behoten'', earlier ''behaten'' (pret. ''behight'', ''behighte'', earlier ''beheht'', ''behet'', pp. ''behoten'', later ''behight''), < AS. ''behātan'' (pret. ''behēt'', pp. ''behāten'') (= OHG. ''bihaizan'', MHG. ''beheizen''), promise, < ''be-'' + ''hātan'', command, call: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''hight''<sup>2</sup>. The forms in ME. were confused, like those of the simple verb. The proper sense of ''behight'' is ‘promise’; the other senses (found only in Spenser and contemporary archaists) are forced, being in part taken from ''hight''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To promise; vow.
{{smaller block|<poem>The trayteresse fals and ful of gyle,
That al ''behoteth'' and nothing halt.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 621.}}
''Behight'' by vow unto the chaste Minerve.
{{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To call; name.
{{smaller block|That Geauntesse Argante is ''behight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 47.}}}}
'''3.''' To address.
readings.c2s1:
'''5.''' To mean; intend.
{{smaller block|Words sometimes mean more than the heart ''behight''.
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', p. 461.}}}}
'''6.''' To commit; intrust.
{{smaller block|The keies are to thy hand ''behight''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 50.}}}}
'''7.''' To adjudge.
{{smaller block|<poem>There was it judged, by those worthie wights,
That Satyrane the first day best had donne: . . .
The second was to Triamond ''behight''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 7.}}}}
'''8.''' To command; ordain.
{{smaller block|<poem>So, taking courteous congé, he ''behight''
Those gates to be unbar’d, and forth he went.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xi. 17.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To address one’s self.
{{smaller block|And lowly to her lowting thus ''behight''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. ii. 38.}}}}

¶
'''behight†''' (bē-hīt′), ''n.'' [< ''behight'', ''v.'' Cf. ME. ''behet'', ''behot'', ''behat'', < AS. ''behāt'', a promise. See ''behest''.] A promise; vow; pledge. ''Surrey''.

'''behind''' (bē-hīnd′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ME. ''behinde'', ''behinden'', < AS. ''behindan'' (= OS. ''bihindan''), adv. and prep., behind, < ''be'', by, + ''hindan'', adv., behind, from behind, at the back: see ''be-''<sup>2</sup> and ''hind''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' At the back of some person or thing; in the rear: opposed to ''before''.
{{smaller block|<poem>So runn’st thou after that which flies from thee,
Whilst I thy babe chase thee afar ''behind''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxliii.}}}}
'''2.''' Toward the back part; backward: as, to look ''behind''.
{{smaller block|<poem>She that could think, and ne’er disclose her mind,
See suitors following, and not look ''behind''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1.}}
Worse things, unheard, unseen, remain ''behind''.}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|behavior|509|beholding}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Even at dancing parties, where it would seem that the poetry of motion might do something to soften the rigid bosom of Venetian ''deportment'', the poor young people separate after each dance. {{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|An elderly gentleman, large and portly and of remarkably dignified ''demeanor'', passing slowly along. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, iv.}}}}

'''behead''' (bẹ̄-hed′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beheden, bihefden, biheveden'', < AS. ''beheáfdian'' (= MHG. ''behoubeten''; cf. G. ''ent-haupten'' = D. ''ont-hoofden''), behead, < ''be-'', here priv., + ''heáfod'', head: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''head.'']   '''1.''' To cut off the head of; kill or execute by decapitation.
{{smaller block|Russell and Sidney were ''beheaded'' in defiance of law and justice. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to deprive of the head, top, or foremost part of: as, to ''behead'' a statue or a word.

'''beheading''' (bẹ̄-hed′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''behead.'']   The act of cutting off the head; specifically, execution by decapitation.
{{smaller block|In Dahomey there are frequent ''beheadings'' that the victims, going to the other world to serve the dead king, may carry messages from his living descendant. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 141.}}}}

'''beheld''' (bẹ̄-held′). Preterit and past participle of ''behold.''

'''behell†''' (bē̤-hel′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hell.'']   To torture as with pains of hell.
{{smaller block|Did ''behell'' and rack him. {{right|''Hewyt.''}}}}

'''behemoth''' (bē̤-hē′mọth), ''n.''   [< Heb. ''b’hemōth'', appar. pl. of excellence, ‘great beast,’ sing. ''b’hēmah'', a beast, but supposed to be an adaptation of Egypt. ''p-ehe-mau'', lit. water-ox.]   An animal mentioned in Job xl. 15-24; probably, from the details given, a hippopotamus, but sometimes taken for some other animal, or for a type of the largest land-animals generally.
{{smaller block|Behold now ''behemoth'', which I made with thee, he eateth grass as an ox. {{right|Job xl. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Behold in plaited mail
''Behemoth'' rears his head.</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Summer, l. 710.}}}}

'''behen, ben'''<sup>6</sup> (bē′hen, ben), ''n.''   [Also written ''beken'', ''been'', appar. a corruption of Ar. ''bahman'', ''behmen'', a kind of root, also the flower ''Rosa canina''.]   An old name of the bladder-campion, ''Silene inflata''. {{smaller|The behen-root of old pharmacists is said to have been the root of ''Centaurea Behen'' and of ''Statice Limonium'', distinguished as ''white'' and ''red behen''.}}

'''behest''' (bē̤-hest′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''behest'', ''bihest'', ''beheste'', etc., with excrescent ''t'', earlier ''behese'', < late AS. ''behǣs'', a promise, vow (equiv. to ''behāt'' = OHG. ''biheiz'', a promise; cf. ''behight'', ''n''.), < ''behātan'', promise: see ''behight'', ''v''., and ''hest''.]   '''1†.''' A vow; a promise. ''Chaucer''; ''Gower'';   ''Holland''.—'''2.''' A command; precept; mandate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where I have learn’d me to repent the sin
Of disobedient opposition
To you and your ''behests''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 2.}}}}
<poem>He did not pause to parley nor protest,
But hastened to obey the Lord’s ''behest.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Longfellow'', Torquemada.}}}}

'''behest†''' (bē-hest′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''behesten'', promise, < ''beheste'', a promise: see ''behest'', ''n.'']   To promise; vow.

'''behete†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''behight.''

'''behew†''', ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''behewen'', hew about, carve, < AS. ''beheáwan'', hew off, < ''be-'' (in AS. priv.) + ''heáwan'', cut, hew.]   To carve; adorn; embellish.
{{smaller block|Al with gold ''behewe.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1306.}}}}

'''behight†''' (bē-hīt′), ''v.''   [The common spelling in Spenser and his contemporaries of both present and preterit of ME. pres. inf. ''beheten'', regularly ''behoten'', earlier ''behaten'' (pret. ''behight'', ''behighte'', earlier ''beheht'', ''behet'', pp. ''behoten'', later ''behight''), < AS. ''behātan'' (pret. ''behēt'', pp. ''behāten'') (= OHG. ''bihaizan'', MHG. ''beheizen''), promise, < ''be-'' + ''hātan'', command, call: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''hight''<sup>2</sup>. The forms in ME. were confused, like those of the simple verb. The proper sense of ''behight'' is ‘promise’; the other senses (found only in Spenser and contemporary archaists) are forced, being in part taken from ''hight''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To promise; vow.
{{smaller block|<poem>The trayteresse fals and ful of gyle,
That al ''behoteth'' and nothing halt.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 621.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Behight'' by vow unto the chaste Minerve.
{{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To call; name.
{{smaller block|That Geauntesse Argante is ''behight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 47.}}}}
'''3.''' To address. {{smaller block|Whom soone as he beheld he knew, and thus ''behight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. iv. 25.}}}}
'''4.''' To pronounce; declare to be.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why of late
Didst thou ''behight'' me borne of English blood?</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 64.}}}} '''5.''' To mean; intend.
{{smaller block|Words sometimes mean more than the heart ''behight''.
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', p. 461.}}}}
'''6.''' To commit; intrust.
{{smaller block|The keies are to thy hand ''behight''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 50.}}}}
'''7.''' To adjudge.
{{smaller block|<poem>There was it judged, by those worthie wights,
That Satyrane the first day best had donne: . . .
The second was to Triamond ''behight''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 7.}}}}
'''8.''' To command; ordain.
{{smaller block|<poem>So, taking courteous congé, he ''behight''
Those gates to be unbar’d, and forth he went.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xi. 17.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To address one’s self.
{{smaller block|And lowly to her lowting thus ''behight''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. ii. 38.}}}}

'''behight†''' (bē-hīt′), ''n.''   [< ''behight'', ''v.'' Cf. ME. ''behet'', ''behot'', ''behat'', < AS. ''behāt'', a promise. See ''behest''.]   A promise; vow; pledge.   ''Surrey''.

'''behind''' (bē-hīnd′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [< ME. ''behinde'', ''behinden'', < AS. ''behindan'' (= OS. ''bihindan''), adv. and prep., behind, < ''be'', by, + ''hindan'', adv., behind, from behind, at the back: see ''be-''<sup>2</sup> and ''hind''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' At the back of some person or thing; in the rear: opposed to ''before''.
{{smaller block|<poem>So runn’st thou after that which flies from thee,
Whilst I thy babe chase thee afar ''behind''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxliii.}}}}
'''2.''' Toward the back part; backward: as, to look ''behind''.
{{smaller block|<poem>She that could think, and ne’er disclose her mind,
See suitors following, and not look ''behind''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Worse things, unheard, unseen, remain ''behind''. {{right|''Shelley'', Prometheus Unbound, i. 1.}}}}

'''3.''' Out of sight; not produced or exhibited to view; in abeyance or reserve.

{{smaller block|And fill up that which is ''behind'' of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh. {{right|Col. i. 24.}}}}
{{smaller block|We cannot be sure that there is no evidence ''behind''.
{{right|''Locke''.}}}}

'''4.''' Remaining after some occurrence, action, or operation: as, he departed and left us ''behind''.

{{smaller block|<poem>Thou shalt live in this fair world ''behind''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Where the bee can suck no honey, she leaves her sting ''behind''.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Prol. to Knight of Burning Pestle.}}}}

'''5.''' Past in the progress of time.

{{smaller block|Forgetting those things which are ''behind''. Phil. iii. 13.}}

'''6.''' In arrear; behindhand: as, he is ''behind'' in his rent.

{{smaller block|So that ye come ''behind'' in no gift. {{right|1 Cor. i. 7.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' At the back or in the rear of, as regards either the actual or the assumed front: the opposite of ''before'': as, the valet stood ''behind'' his master; crouching ''behind'' a tree.

<poem>''Behind'' yon hills where Lugar flows.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Burns'', My Nannie, O.}}}}
<poem>A tall Brabanter ''behind'' whom I stood.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Account of Himself.}}}}
<poem>The lion walk’d along
''Behind'' some hedge.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1094.}}}}

'''2.''' Figuratively, in a position or at a point not so far advanced as; in the rear of, as regards progress, knowledge, development, etc.; not on an equality with: as, ''behind'' the age; he is ''behind'' the others in mathematics.

{{smaller block|For I suppose I was not a whit ''behind'' the very chiefest apostles.
{{right|2 Cor. xi. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|In my devotion to the Union I hope I am ''behind'' no man in the nation.
{{right|''Lincoln'', in Raymond, p. 99.}}}}
'''3.''' In existence or remaining after the removal or disappearance of: as, he left a large family ''behind'' him.
{{smaller block|What he gave me to publish was but a small part of what he left ''behind'' him.
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Behind one’s back.''' See ''back''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Behind the curtain.''' See ''curtain.''—'''Behind the scenes.''' See ''scene.''—'''Behind the times,''' not well informed as to current events; holding to older ideas and ways.—'''Behind time,''' later than the proper or appointed time in doing anything. ='''Syn.''' ''Behind, After. Behind'' relates primarily to position; ''after'', to time. When ''after'' notes position, it is less close or exact than ''behind'', and it means position in motion. To say that men stood one ''after'' another in a line was once correct (see ''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 901, “kneeled . . . each ''after'' other”), but is not so now. They may come one ''after'' another, that is, somewhat irregularly and apart; they came one ''behind'' another, that is, close together, one covering another. The distinction is similar to that between ''beneath'' and ''below''.}}
{{smaller block|Out bounced a splendidly spotted creature of the cat kind. Immediately ''behind'' him crept out his mate; and there they stood.
{{right|''P. Robinson'', Under the Sun, p. 144.}}}}
{{smaller block|On him they laid the cross, that he might bear it ''after'' Jesus.
{{right|Luke xxiii. 26.}}}}

'''behindhand''' (bē-hīnd′hand), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''   [< ''behind'' + ''hand''; cf. ''beforehand.'']   '''1.''' In the rear; in a backward state; not sufficiently advanced; not equally advanced with some other person or thing: as, ''behindhand'' in studies or work.
{{smaller block|<poem>And these thy offices,
So rarely kind, are as interpreters
Of my ''behind-hand'' slackness.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Up, and all the morning within doors, beginning to set my accounts in order from before this fire, I being ''behind-hand'' with them ever since.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 480.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nothing can exceed the evils of this spring. All agricultural operations are at least a month ''behindhand.''
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', To Lady Holland.}}}}
'''2.''' Late; delayed beyond the proper time; behind the time set or expected.
{{smaller block|Government expeditions are generally ''behindhand.''
{{right|''Cornhill Mag.'', March, 1862.}}}}
'''3.''' In a state in which expenditure has gone beyond income; in a state in which means are not adequate to the supply of wants; in arrear: as, to be ''behindhand'' in one’s circumstances; you are ''behindhand'' with your payments.
{{smaller block|Having run something ''behindhand'' in the world, he obtained the favour of a certain lord to receive him into his house.
{{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, ii.}}}}
'''4.''' Underhand; secret; clandestine. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Those ''behindhand'' and paltry manœuvres which destroy confidence between human beings and degrade the character of the statesman and the man.
{{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., xv.}}}}

'''behither†''' (bē-hiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''prep.''   [< ''be-''<sup>2</sup> as in ''beyond'', ''behind'', etc., + ''hither.'']   On this side of.
{{smaller block|Two miles ''behither'' Clifden.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, July 23, 1679.}}}}

'''behold''' (bē̤-hōld′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''beheld'', ppr. ''beholding''.   [< ME. ''beholden'', ''biholdan'', ''bihalden'', hold, bind by obligation (in this sense only in pp. ''beholden'', ''beholde'': see ''beholden''), commonly observe, see, < AS. ''behealdan'', hold, keep, observe, see (= OS. ''bihaldan'' = OFries. ''bihalda'' = D. ''behouden'' = OHG. ''bihaltan'', MHG. G. ''behalten'', keep), < ''be-'' + ''healdan'', hold, keep: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''hold''<sup>1</sup>. Other words combining the senses ‘keep’ and ‘look at’ are ''observe'' and ''regard''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To hold by; keep; retain.—'''2†.''' To hold; keep; observe (a command).—'''3.''' To hold in view; fix the eyes upon; look at; see with attention; observe with care.
{{smaller block|When he ''beheld'' the serpent of brass, he lived.
{{right|Num. xxi. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Behold'' the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
{{right|John i. 29.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Observe'', ''Witness'', etc. (see ''see''); look upon, consider, eye, view, survey, contemplate, regard.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To look; direct the eyes to an object; view; see: in a physical sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Virginius gan upon the cherl ''beholde''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Doctor’s Tale, l. 191.}}}}
{{smaller block|And I ''beheld'', and lo, in the midst of the throne . . . stood a Lamb as it had been slain.
{{right|Rev. v. 6.}}}}
'''2.''' To fix the attention upon an object; attend; direct or fix the mind: in this sense used chiefly in the imperative, being frequently little more than an exclamation calling attention, or expressive of wonder, admiration, and the like.
{{smaller block|''Behold'', I stand at the door and knock.
{{right|Rev. iii. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Prithee, see there! ''behold!'' look! lo!</poem>}}
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4.}}}}
'''3†.''' To feel obliged or bound.
{{smaller block|For who would ''behold'' to geue counsell, if in counselling there should be any perill?
{{right|''J. Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, iii.}}}}

'''beholden''' (bẹ̄-hōl′dn), ''p. a.''   [Formerly often erroneously ''beholding''; < ME. ''beholden'', ''beholde'', prop. ppr. of ''behold'', ''v.'']   Obliged; bound in gratitude; indebted; held by obligation.
{{smaller block|Little are we ''beholden'' to your love.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|We had classics of our own, without being ''beholden'' to “insolent Greece or haughty Rome.”
{{right|''Lamb'', Christ’s Hospital.}}}}

'''beholder''' (bẹ̄-hōl′dėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''beholder'', ''biholder'', ''-ere''; < ''behold'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who beholds; a spectator; one who looks upon or sees.
{{smaller block|<poem>Was this the face
That, like the sun, did make ''beholders'' wink?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1.}}}}

'''beholding'''<sup>1</sup> (bẹ̄-hōl′ding), ''n.''   [< ME. ''beholdynge'', ''bihaldunge''; < ''beholden'', behold.]   The act of looking at; gaze; view; sight.
{{smaller block|The revenges we are bound to take upon your traitorous father are not fit for your ''beholding''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 7.}}}}

'''beholding'''<sup>2</sup>† (bẹ̄-hōl′ding), ''a.''   [Corrupt form of ''beholden''.]   '''1.''' Under obligation; obliged.
{{smaller block|The stage is more ''beholding'' to love than the life of man.
{{right|''Bacon'', Love.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
